titleText.es: Es difícil caber en el asiento de atrás con mi androide RealDoll cuando ambos llevamos puestos los jetpacks.
titleText.en: It's hard to fit in the backseat of my flying car with my android Realdoll when we're both wearing jetpacks.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish title text is preserved exactly from the archive, including the branded names RealDoll and jetpacks. The English field preserves the official title text. The Spanish raster localizes the official 3D shooter more generally as VIDEOJUEGO 3D and names ANGRY BIRDS in the final warning; those technical and game-title labels, plus the year 2011, are audited exclusions. OCR's PAR, UGAR, 31, INTERRUMPI, and Tio are corrected to the visible PARA, JUGAR, 3D, INTERRUMPÍ, and TÍO.

regions.labelEs: ESTAMOS EN 2011. QUIERO MI COCHE VOLADOR.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed calendar year is a number rather than Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Volador follows coche in the common neutral descriptive order.
Volador uses the masculine singular ending to match coche.

regions.labelEs: TE ESTÁS QUEJANDO DESDE UN TELÉFONO CON EL QUE HACES COMPRAS Y LEES LIBROS.

applications.explanationEn: Estás matches one familiar listener, and quejando supplies the ongoing complaint; te separately marks the pronominal verb.
Con supplies the relationship, el matches the masculine teléfono, and que links back to it.
Haces matches one familiar listener, and compras names the shopping activity.

regions.labelEs: Y QUE ESTABAS USANDO PARA JUGAR A UN VIDEOJUEGO 3D HASTA QUE TE INTERRUMPÍ CON LO QUE HUBIERA SIDO UNA VIDEOLLAMADA SI LLEVARA PUESTA UNA CAMISETA.

excludedUnits.rationale: This dimensional label is technical notation rather than Spanish lexical vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Que continues the description of the earlier phone, while estabas usando supplies the complete action that describes it.
Estabas matches one familiar listener in past background time, and usando supplies the ongoing action.
Estabas uses the imperfect to frame the listener's use as background already in progress.
Para introduces the purpose, and jugar remains in its dictionary form.
Jugar names the activity, a provides its required link, and un videojuego fills the game slot.
Hasta que introduces a completed factual endpoint, and interrumpí uses an ordinary completed-past statement form.
Interrumpí uses the preterite to present the interruption as the completed event that advances the story.
Lo and que refer neutrally to the unnamed thing or situation described next.

applications.exampleEs: HUBIERA SIDO UNA VIDEOLLAMADA SI LLEVARA
applications.explanationEn: Hubiera plus sido supplies the imagined earlier result; si introduces the unreal present condition, whose verb llevara uses the special -ra form.
Llevara supplies the imagined form of llevar, and puesta matches the feminine clothing noun camiseta.
Puesta uses its feminine singular ending to match camiseta.

regions.labelEs: ¿NO PUEDO TENER TAMBIÉN UN COCHE VOLADOR?

applications.explanationEn: Puedo asks about the speaker's permission, while tener remains in its unchanged dictionary form.

applications.exampleEs: NO PUEDO TENER TAMBIÉN UN COCHE VOLADOR
applications.explanationEn: Question marks and intonation turn the otherwise statement-shaped words into a yes-or-no request.
Volador follows coche in neutral descriptive order.
Volador uses the masculine singular ending to match coche.

regions.labelEs: TE ESTRELLARÍAS TECLEANDO O JUGANDO AL ANGRY BIRDS.

excludedUnits.rationale: This printed English video-game title is a single non-Spanish lexical unit.

applications.explanationEn: Estrellarías keeps the dictionary-form stem and adds the informal-singular conditional ending -ías.
The -ando form presents typing or texting as an action happening at the same time as the crash risk.
The -ando form presents game-playing as the other simultaneous action.
Jugando is the game-playing form, and a + el contracts to al before the printed game title.

cards.noteEn: Before a specific moment, en can correspond to English “at.”

example.en: He arrived at just the right moment.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

example.en: I need a new backpack.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.promptEs: coche volador · teléfono · videojuego · videollamada · estrellarse
cards.questionEn: Why does the reply argue that a flying car would be unsafe despite impressive modern technology?
cards.answerEn: The phone already combines shopping, books, 3D games, and video calls, but the user's distraction by that same device would make a flying car dangerous.
cards.noteEn: The complaint treats flying cars as the missing sign of the future while ignoring capabilities that already arrived in a handheld device. The final warning turns that wonder into a safety problem: typing or gaming while piloting would add airborne consequences to familiar distracted-driving behavior.

example.es: La tecnología nueva no elimina el riesgo de usarla sin atención.
example.en: New technology does not remove the risk of using it inattentively.

cards.noteEn: Volador describes something that flies or is designed to fly. It changes to voladora with a feminine singular noun and adds -es in the plural.

example.en: They designed a flying vehicle.

cards.noteEn: Tío literally means “uncle,” but in casual speech in Spain it can address a male friend much like “dude” or “man.”

example.es: Tío, no me lo puedo creer.
example.en: Dude, I can't believe it.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word here; marks a “you” verb used with te
cards.noteEn: Some Spanish verbs use te when the person affected is the informal listener. The meaning belongs to the whole verb pattern, so English may not translate te separately.

example.en: You stay here.

cards.answerEn: Use a form of estar followed by an action word ending in -ando or -iendo.
cards.noteEn: Estar changes to show who is doing the action: estoy, estás, está, and so on. For most verbs, replace -ar with -ando (hablar → hablando) and replace -er or -ir with -iendo (comer → comiendo, vivir → viviendo). This is similar to English “am/is/are doing.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone is in the middle of doing something?

example.en: I am reading.

cards.noteEn: Quejando is the -ando form used inside quejarse, “to complain.” Its matching marker appears separately before a conjugated helper: te estás quejando.

example.es: Siempre se está quejando del ruido.
example.en: He is always complaining about the noise.

cards.noteEn: Teléfono is stressed on lé, which is why it carries a written accent.

example.en: The phone is ringing.

cards.questionEn: How do you say forms such as “in which,” “with whom,” or “for whom” when referring back to a person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Put the needed preposition before el que, la que, los que, or las que, matching the earlier person or thing.
cards.noteEn: A preposition is a short relationship word such as en (“in”), con (“with”), or para (“for”). Choose el, la, los, or las to match the gender and number of the person or thing being described; que itself does not change. English may use “which” for a thing or “who” or “whom” for a person.

example.es: Esta es la silla en la que me siento.
example.en: This is the chair that I sit in.

cards.answerEn: the masculine article inside el que (‘which’)
cards.noteEn: After a linking word such as en, el que can refer back to one masculine thing. El matches that earlier thing, while que introduces the added information.

example.es: Ese es el libro en el que aparece la foto.
example.en: That is the book in which the photo appears.

cards.noteEn: Que connects a noun to information describing it. Depending on the noun, English translates it as “who,” “that,” or “which.”

example.es: La persona que llamó es mi amiga.
example.en: The person who called is my friend.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone shops or makes purchases?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of hacer followed by compras.
cards.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time: hago compras, haces compras, hicimos compras. Compras remains plural and names the shopping activity or purchases.

example.en: We do our shopping on Saturdays.

cards.noteEn: Compras is the plural of compra. In hacer compras, it refers to shopping or making purchases.

example.es: Hicimos las compras por la mañana.
example.en: We did the shopping in the morning.

cards.noteEn: Lees is the present form of leer for one familiar listener.

example.en: You read many books.

cards.noteEn: Libros is the masculine plural of libro.

example.en: These books are new.

cards.questionEn: How do you add information about a named person or thing using “who,” “that,” or “which”?
cards.answerEn: Put que after the person or thing, then add a verb and the information about it.
cards.noteEn: Que links the added description to the person or thing before it. It does not change for masculine, feminine, singular, or plural nouns. The added part needs a verb: la casa que vimos means “the house that we saw.”

example.es: La casa que vimos es azul.
example.en: The house that we saw is blue.

cards.answerEn: you were (helper for an action in progress)
cards.noteEn: Estabas is the informal-singular imperfect form of estar. Before an -ando or -iendo form, it presents what the listener was doing in the background.

example.en: You were reading when I called.

cards.answerEn: Use the preterite for a completed event and the imperfect for background, an ongoing situation, or something that used to happen.
cards.noteEn: Think of a story: the preterite answers “What happened next?” The imperfect answers “What was happening?”, “What were things like?”, or “What used to happen?” These two names describe how the speaker presents an event, not simply how long it lasted.
cards.questionEn: Spanish has two common ways to talk about the past. When do you use each one?

example.en: While I was walking, it started to rain.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Jugar means taking part in a game. It is commonly followed by a before the game or activity.

example.en: We are going to play chess.

cards.questionEn: How do you name the game that someone plays?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of jugar, then a, then the game.
cards.noteEn: Jugar changes for the player and time. A links it to the game. If the game has masculine article el, a + el must contract to al: jugar al tenis. With an indefinite article, keep a un or a una.

example.es: Marta juega a un juego de cartas y Luis juega al tenis.
example.en: Marta plays a card game and Luis plays tennis.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; required after jugar before a game
cards.noteEn: When jugar names the game being played, Spanish normally uses a before it. Before el, a and el combine as al.

example.es: Los niños juegan a un juego nuevo.
example.en: The children play a new game.

cards.noteEn: Videojuego combines vídeo and juego into the standard word for an electronic game.

example.en: They bought a cooperative video game.

cards.promptEs: hasta que + hecho habitual o conocido
cards.questionEn: What verb form follows hasta que for a usual or already-known event?
cards.answerEn: Use an ordinary statement form when the event is habitual, known, or already completed.
cards.noteEn: Hasta que means “until.” Spanish uses an ordinary statement form for an event treated as a fact. A still-awaited future event instead uses the special subjunctive form; for example, llega is an ordinary form, while llegue is the corresponding subjunctive form.

example.es: Siempre leo hasta que empieza la clase.
example.en: I always read until class starts.

cards.noteEn: Interrumpí is the completed-past form of interrumpir for the speaker. The written accent marks the stressed final syllable.

example.en: I interrupted the meeting by mistake.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Lo combines with que to refer to an idea, action, or whole situation rather than a masculine noun. Together, lo que means “what” or “the thing that.”

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.questionEn: How do you say “what” or “the thing that” without naming a specific object?
cards.answerEn: Use lo que to refer to an idea, action, situation, or unnamed thing.
cards.noteEn: Here lo is neutral: it does not stand for a masculine noun. Que introduces the information that identifies the idea or thing. Together they work as one unit.

example.en: I don't understand what you're saying.

cards.answerEn: what; that which (as part of lo que)
cards.noteEn: Here que completes lo que, a neutral expression meaning “what” or “the thing that.” It does not refer to a particular masculine or feminine noun.

example.en: I understand what you’re saying.

cards.noteEn: Hubiera is a special past form of haber. In a counterfactual result, it can combine with a completed-action form as an accepted alternative to habría: hubiera sido can mean “would have been.”

example.en: It would have been better to wait.

cards.promptEs: hubiera + participio ... si + forma hipotética en -ra
cards.questionEn: How can you say that an unreal situation now would have produced a different earlier result, using hubiera?
cards.answerEn: Use hubiera plus a completed-action form for the imagined result, and use si plus a special -ra form for the unreal current condition.
cards.noteEn: The condition's -ra form is called the imperfect subjunctive: tener becomes tuviera. The result uses the past subjunctive helper hubiera plus a participle, a completed-action form such as ido or visto. In result clauses, this hubiera form is an accepted alternative to habría: hubiera ido and habría ido can both mean “would have gone.”

example.es: Hubiera ido contigo si tuviera tiempo.
example.en: I would have gone with you if I had time.

cards.noteEn: Sido is the completed-action form of ser. It follows a form of haber: ha sido means “has been,” and haber sido means “to have been.”

example.en: It must have been difficult.

cards.noteEn: Videollamada combines vídeo and llamada for a call in which participants can see one another.

example.es: Tenemos una videollamada a las tres.
example.en: We have a video call at three.

cards.answerEn: were wearing; had on (in an unreal condition)
cards.noteEn: Llevara is a special -ra form of llevar used for an imagined condition. With puesto or puesta, it describes clothing that someone has on.

example.es: Si llevara abrigo, no tendría frío.
example.en: If I were wearing a coat, I would not be cold.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone has an item of clothing on?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of llevar followed by puesto, puesta, puestos, or puestas and the clothing item.
cards.noteEn: Llevar changes for the wearer and time. Puesto changes to match the clothing noun in gender and number: lleva puesto un abrigo, lleva puestas unas botas.

example.en: Ana is wearing a hat.

cards.noteEn: Puesta follows a form of llevar to describe clothing being worn. It matches the clothing noun: puesto for masculine singular and puesta for feminine singular.

example.en: She is wearing a blue jacket.

cards.noteEn: Camiseta usually names a T-shirt or light casual shirt.

example.en: He is wearing a white T-shirt.

cards.questionEn: How can Spanish turn an ordinary statement into a yes-or-no question?
cards.answerEn: Use question marks and questioning intonation; Spanish does not need a separate helper like English do or does.
cards.noteEn: The word order can remain the same as in a statement, especially in conversation. The opening and closing question marks show the question in writing.

example.en: Do they have coffee?

cards.noteEn: Puedo is the form of poder for the speaker. In a question, it can ask whether an action is allowed rather than whether the speaker is capable of doing it.

example.en: May I use the bathroom?

cards.promptEs: poder + verbo en forma de diccionario
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone can, could, or may do something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of poder for the person and situation, then keep the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: Poder changes to forms such as puedo, puedes, puede, podemos, and pueden for present ability or possibility. Podría can present a possible or imagined option. The following action keeps its -ar, -er, or -ir ending.

example.en: We can enter now.

cards.noteEn: Estrellarías is the conditional form used with te for the pronominal verb estrellarse, “to crash.” The ending -ías marks one familiar listener.

example.en: Without brakes, you would crash.

cards.questionEn: How do you form a Spanish “would” verb such as “would forget”?
cards.answerEn: Keep the whole dictionary form and add a conditional ending such as -ía.
cards.noteEn: The same endings attach to verbs ending in -ar, -er, and -ir. The ending changes for the person: -ía, -ías, -ía, -íamos, -íais, or -ían.

example.en: We would travel by train.

cards.noteEn: Tecleando is the -ando form of teclear, pressing keys to enter text. Context can make it typing at a keyboard or texting on a phone.

example.en: She crossed the street while texting.

cards.promptEs: -ando / -iendo para una acción simultánea o un medio
cards.questionEn: How can you add an action that happens at the same time or explains how something is done?
cards.answerEn: Use the action form ending in -ando or -iendo, such as hablando or corriendo.
cards.noteEn: Spanish calls this form the gerund. It does not change for the person. Used on its own, it can describe a simultaneous action or the means used: Entró corriendo means the person entered by running. This differs from estar plus the same form, which focuses on an action in progress.

example.en: She came in running.

cards.noteEn: Jugando is the -ando form of jugar. It can name a simultaneous action and is followed by a before the game being played.

example.es: Pasó la tarde jugando al dominó.
example.en: He spent the afternoon playing dominoes.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

example.en: I’m going to the market.
